Kopia process spawns ssh with -oProxyCommand= argument (CVE-2026-45695) AIExploitation High
Detects exploitation of Kopia's unauthenticated SFTP/externalSSH path injection. When the vulnerable /api/v1/repo/exists handler invokes blob.NewStorage with attacker-supplied sshArguments, the kopia process directly forks ssh with a -oProxyCommand= token that OpenSSH then executes via $SHELL -c. The kopia→ssh parent/child with ProxyCommand in the child argv is a near-zero-FP signature of this RCE. Rationale: Uses the exact narrow signature described in the advisory: kopia process (vulnerable handler) directly invoking exec.CommandContext("ssh", ...) with a ProxyCommand token. The string 'ProxyCommand' in an ssh argv whose parent is kopia has effectively no benign use case outside intentional SFTP jump-host setups. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory, the Kopia v0.22.3 source references in the article, and the fix PR #5354. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/kopia/kopia/pull/5354 • https://github.com/kopia/kopia/blob/v0.22.3/repo/blob/sftp/sftp_storage.go • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-45695
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Kopia operator manually configuring an SFTP repository through a corporate SSH bastion using ProxyCommand
  • Internal automation/Ansible role that sets up Kopia SFTP backends with a documented ProxyCommand to traverse network segmentation
  • Backup admin testing externalSSH SFTP configuration against an internal hardened jump host
  • Red-team exercise simulating CVE-2026-45695 exploitation
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName in~ ("backup-bastion-01","backup-bastion-02") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "server start" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--tls-cert" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bastion.internal","jump.corp.local"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Capture the full child ssh command line and any subsequent child processes of that ssh PID (look for /bin/sh -c, bash -c, cmd.exe /c). Pull the kopia HTTP access log for the same host around the event time and grep for POST /api/v1/repo/exists; capture the source IP. Confirm whether kopia was started with --without-password and bound to a non-loopback interface. Step 2 (contain): Stop the kopia server process immediately, block inbound to the Kopia HTTP port (default 51515) at the host firewall, and isolate the host if any shell child of ssh was observed. Rotate any credentials/keys reachable from the kopia process user. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all hosts running kopia <= 0.22.3 for the same parent/child pattern over the last 30 days, query egress for the kopia HTTP port from untrusted networks, and review the kopia process user's bash/zsh history and crontabs for persistence dropped during the window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("kopia","kopia.exe","kopia-ui","kopia-ui.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("ssh","ssh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "ProxyCommand"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessId, InitiatingProcessId, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("kopia","kopia.exe","kopia-ui","kopia-ui.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ssh","ssh.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "ProxyCommand"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Kopia Spawning SSH with ProxyCommand Argument (CVE-2026-45695)
id: 7c6f8e2a-3b21-4d8b-b9f6-9a4d0c1f5e21
description: Detects exploitation of Kopia CVE-2026-45695 where the unauthenticated /api/v1/repo/exists handler triggers the kopia process to invoke ssh with an attacker-controlled -oProxyCommand= argument, leading to command execution as the kopia user.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2q4c-3mrw-63c3

logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/kopia'
      - '\kopia.exe'
      - '/kopia-ui'
      - '\kopia-ui.exe'
  selection_child:

falsepositives:

level: critical

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^kopia(-ui)?(\.exe)?$/i ImageFileName=/[\\\/]ssh(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("(?i)proxycommand", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

SSH process spawned by Kopia invokes a shell child (ProxyCommand execution) AIInstallation High
Detects the second-stage execution arm of CVE-2026-45695: OpenSSH evaluates -oProxyCommand=<cmd> by invoking $SHELL -c <cmd> before any TCP connect. The resulting kopia → ssh → (sh|bash|cmd|powershell) grand-parent/parent/child chain is the artifact of arbitrary code running as the kopia service account. Rationale: This is the exact execution chain the advisory describes — OpenSSH spawns $SHELL -c <attacker_cmd> before attempting TCP, so the shell child of ssh is the observable smoking gun. Pairing it with a kopia grand-parent (via SshPid join) removes essentially all benign ssh ProxyCommand use. Confirmed against the GHSA advisory text and OpenSSH ProxyCommand documented behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2q4c-3mrw-63c3 • https://man.openbsd.org/ssh_config.5#ProxyCommand • https://github.com/kopia/kopia/pull/5354
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Kopia SFTP backend deliberately configured with ProxyCommand=nc/corkscrew through a corporate proxy
  • Backup admin manually launching ssh via the kopia CLI session with a ProxyCommand for jump-host traversal
  • Misconfigured backup automation that wraps ssh with a netcat-based tunnel
  • Diagnostic ssh invocation by the kopia process user during troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("corkscrew","nc -X","connect-proxy") and DeviceName startswith "backup-")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Capture the ShellCmd value — this is the literal attacker payload. Resolve the source IP of the originating POST /api/v1/repo/exists in the kopia application log and the Kopia HTTP port's network logs. Verify Kopia version is <= 0.22.3 and check for --without-password flag in the kopia systemd unit / launch args. Step 2 (contain): Kill the spawned shell PID and any descendants, stop the kopia service, firewall-block the Kopia HTTP listener from non-loopback, and put the host into containment if the shell ran anything beyond a no-op probe. Preserve memory and the kopia binary for forensics. Step 3 (hunt): Search 30 days of process telemetry for ssh→shell children whose ssh grand-parent was kopia. Pivot on the kopia service user to find any new cron entries, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys mutations, SUID drops, or outbound C2 connections. Identify all internet-reachable Kopia instances in the org and confirm patch status.

    DeviceProcessEvents

    | where FileName in~ ("ssh","ssh.exe")
    | project SshTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, SshPid = ProcessId, SshCmd = ProcessCommandLine, KopiaCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ssh","ssh.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","pwsh")
| join kind=inner kopia_ssh on $left.DeviceId == $right.DeviceId and $left.InitiatingProcessId == $right.SshPid
| where Timestamp between (SshTime .. SshTime + 30s)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, KopiaCmd, SshCmd, ShellImage = FolderPath, ShellCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SshPid
| order by Timestamp desc
let kopia_ssh =
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ssh","ssh.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","pwsh")

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),

| order by conn_count desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "3de04fe2a76262743ed089efa7115f4508619838e77d60b9a1aab8b20d2cc8bf", "85f54c089d78ebfb101454ec934c767065a342a43c9ee1beac8430cdd3b2086f", "c0b094e46842260936d4b97ce63e4539b99a3eae48b736798c700217c52569dc") or SHA1 in~ ("069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "3de04fe2a76262743ed089efa7115f4508619838e77d60b9a1aab8b20d2cc8bf", "85f54c089d78ebfb101454ec934c767065a342a43c9ee1beac8430cdd3b2086f", "c0b094e46842260936d4b97ce63e4539b99a3eae48b736798c700217c52569dc") or MD5 in~ ("069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "3de04fe2a76262743ed089efa7115f4508619838e77d60b9a1aab8b20d2cc8bf", "85f54c089d78ebfb101454ec934c767065a342a43c9ee1beac8430cdd3b2086f", "c0b094e46842260936d4b97ce63e4539b99a3eae48b736798c700217c52569dc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "3de04fe2a76262743ed089efa7115f4508619838e77d60b9a1aab8b20d2cc8bf", "85f54c089d78ebfb101454ec934c767065a342a43c9ee1beac8430cdd3b2086f", "c0b094e46842260936d4b97ce63e4539b99a3eae48b736798c700217c52569dc") or SHA1 in~ ("069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "3de04fe2a76262743ed089efa7115f4508619838e77d60b9a1aab8b20d2cc8bf", "85f54c089d78ebfb101454ec934c767065a342a43c9ee1beac8430cdd3b2086f", "c0b094e46842260936d4b97ce63e4539b99a3eae48b736798c700217c52569dc") or MD5 in~ ("069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "3de04fe2a76262743ed089efa7115f4508619838e77d60b9a1aab8b20d2cc8bf", "85f54c089d78ebfb101454ec934c767065a342a43c9ee1beac8430cdd3b2086f", "c0b094e46842260936d4b97ce63e4539b99a3eae48b736798c700217c52569dc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "3de04fe2a76262743ed089efa7115f4508619838e77d60b9a1aab8b20d2cc8bf", "85f54c089d78ebfb101454ec934c767065a342a43c9ee1beac8430cdd3b2086f", "c0b094e46842260936d4b97ce63e4539b99a3eae48b736798c700217c52569dc"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Installation of malicious guardrails-ai==0.10.1 PyPI package (CVE-2026-45758)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Python process executing transformers.pyz dropped from git-tanstack.com (TeamPCP)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS lookup for git-tanstack.com TeamPCP C2 staging domain · [LLM] Outbound connection to TeamPCP C2 IP 83.142.209.194 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Installation of malicious guardrails-ai==0.10.1 PyPI package (CVE-2026-45758) AIDelivery High
Hunts pip/uv/poetry invocations that pin or resolve to the quarantined guardrails-ai 0.10.1 release. Any host that ran this install must be treated as compromised because the malicious code executes on package import, not just install. Rationale: Pivots on the exact malicious release pin string `guardrails-ai==0.10.1` named in the GHSA advisory. SafeDep + Qualys confirm the 0.10.1 PyPI artifact runs malicious code on import; any host that installed it is presumed compromised regardless of whether the dropper fired. Casing variations are covered for path matches. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/guardrails-ai/guardrails/issues/1473 • https://safedep.io/mass-npm-supply-chain-attack-tanstack-mistral/ • https://qualysec.com/cybersecurity-news/mini-shai-hulud-worm-compromises/ • https://www.ox.security/blog/shai-hulud-here-we-go-again-170-packages-hit-across-npm-pypi/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal IR / malware-analysis engineer downloading the quarantined wheel in an isolated VM for triage
  • Build pipelines with a stale requirements.txt that still pins guardrails-ai==0.10.1 (still a true positive — the build host is compromised)
  • Threat-intel platform automation pulling the artifact for sandbox detonation
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("malware-sandbox","ir-vm-","sec-triage-") and AccountName has_any ("ir-","secops-","sandbox-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull `DeviceProcessEvents`/`ProcessRollup2` for the host and confirm whether any `python*` process subsequently imported the package (look for transformers.pyz download in the next 60s). 2) Contain: isolate the device, revoke all credentials reachable from that host (GitHub PATs, cloud SDK creds, AWS/Azure/GCP CLI tokens, npm/PyPI/PAT tokens, kube configs), and treat any CI runner that executed the install as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same SHA256 of the installed wheel across the org, audit GitHub org for unauthorized workflows / repos / new SSH keys, and verify Snowglobe + Guardrails Hub API keys were rotated before 2026-05-13 14:00 PT.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","uv.exe","poetry.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","uv.exe","poetry.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "guardrails-ai" or ProcessCommandLine has "guardrails_ai"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "0.10.1"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 30d;
union isfuzzy=true
(
  SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where NewProcessName has_any ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","uv.exe","poetry.exe")
     or ParentProcessName has_any ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","uv.exe","poetry.exe")
  | where CommandLine has "guardrails-ai" or CommandLine has "guardrails_ai"
  | where CommandLine has "0.10.1"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
),
(
  ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where ActingProcessName has_any ("pip","pip3","python","python3","uv","poetry")
     or TargetProcessName has_any ("pip","pip3","uv","poetry")
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "guardrails-ai" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "guardrails_ai"
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "0.10.1"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, NewProcessName=ActingProcessName, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Installation of Malicious guardrails-ai 0.10.1 PyPI Package (CVE-2026-45758)
id: 8c41a2f9-3b76-4e2d-9e1a-7f1c5a9d4e21
description: Detects pip / uv / poetry / python invocations that install or resolve the malicious guardrails-ai==0.10.1 release published 2026-05-11 (TeamPCP supply-chain attack).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmpw-2vmm-p4p6
  - https://github.com/guardrails-ai/guardrails/issues/1473
  - https://safedep.io/mass-npm-supply-chain-attack-tanstack-mistral/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/20
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_tool:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\pip.exe'
      - '\pip3.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'
      - '\uv.exe'
      - '\poetry.exe'
      - '/pip'
      - '/pip3'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/uv'
      - '/poetry'
  selection_pkg:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'guardrails-ai==0.10.1'
      - 'guardrails-ai-0.10.1'
      - 'guardrails_ai-0.10.1'
      - 'guardrails-ai 0.10.1'
  condition: selection_tool and selection_pkg
falsepositives:
  - Intentional analyst download of the quarantined artifact in an isolated reverse-engineering sandbox
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:windows.security OR source:linux.auditd) (@Image:(*\\pip.exe OR *\\pip3.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\python3.exe OR *\\uv.exe OR *\\poetry.exe) OR @process.executable.path:(*/pip OR */pip3 OR */python OR */python3 OR */uv OR */poetry)) AND (@CommandLine:(*guardrails-ai==0.10.1* OR *guardrails-ai-0.10.1* OR *guardrails_ai-0.10.1*) OR @process.command_line:(*guardrails-ai==0.10.1* OR *guardrails-ai-0.10.1* OR *guardrails_ai-0.10.1*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/(pip|pip3|python|python3|pythonw|uv|poetry)(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("guardrails[-_]ai[ =-]+0\.10\.1", field=CommandLine, flags="i")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName], function=collect([CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName]))
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("pip.exe","pip","pip3","pip3.exe","uv","uv.exe","poetry","poetry.exe","python.exe","python","python3","python3.exe") OR Processes.process IN ("*pip*install*","*uv*pip*install*","*poetry*add*")) AND Processes.process IN ("*guardrails-ai==0.10.1*","*guardrails-ai 0.10.1*","*guardrails_ai-0.10.1*","*guardrails-ai-0.10.1*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Python process executing transformers.pyz dropped from git-tanstack.com (TeamPCP) AIInstallation High
Hunts the post-import dropper stage: a python interpreter invoked with the staged payload filename `transformers.pyz` or writing that file to disk. This is the second-stage execution from the malicious guardrails-ai 0.10.1 __init__.py and is shared with the broader TanStack/Mistral mini-Shai-Hulud campaign. Rationale: SafeDep + Qualys reverse-engineered the malicious `guardrails/__init__.py` and identified the exact dropper filename `transformers.pyz` pulled from git-tanstack.com and executed via python3. `.pyz` is a Python zipapp — a high-signal extension on a process command line because legitimate transformers (HuggingFace) ships as a wheel, not a zipapp. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/mass-npm-supply-chain-attack-tanstack-mistral/ • https://qualysec.com/cybersecurity-news/mini-shai-hulud-worm-compromises/ • https://www.ox.security/blog/shai-hulud-here-we-go-again-170-packages-hit-across-npm-pypi/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.006 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal data-science team distributing a custom zipapp accidentally named transformers.pyz (collision is extremely unlikely)
  • Malware-analysis sandbox detonating the captured payload for IR
  • Threat-intel YARA-fed download of the artifact for static analysis
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the python process succeeded — pull the next 5 minutes of DeviceNetworkEvents from the same DeviceId and look for connections to 83.142.209.194 or git-tanstack.com. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture the on-disk transformers.pyz before AV deletion, and revoke credentials reachable from that machine (env vars, keychain, ~/.aws, ~/.azure, ~/.gitconfig, ~/.npmrc, ~/.pypirc, GitHub PATs). 3) Hunt: search the same hash across the fleet, audit GitHub org for unauthorised workflow runs / new repos / deploy keys originating from any developer with python history on this host, and compare timeline against any 0.10.1 install events from UC1.
let LookbackDays = 30d;
union isfuzzy=true
(
  DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
     or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "transformers.pyz"
     or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "transformers.pyz"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, ActionType="ProcessCreate"
),
(
  DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where FileName =~ "transformers.pyz"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, ActionType
)
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 30d;
union isfuzzy=true
(
  ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","pythonw")
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "transformers.pyz"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, ProcessName=ActingProcessName, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, Source="ImProcessCreate"
),
(
  SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where NewProcessName has_any ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe")
  | where CommandLine has "transformers.pyz"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, ProcessName=NewProcessName, CommandLine, Source="4688"
),
(
  ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where TargetFileName =~ "transformers.pyz"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, ProcessName=ActingProcessName, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, Source="ImFileEvent"
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DNS lookup for git-tanstack.com TeamPCP C2 staging domain AICommand & Control High
Detects any DNS query for the attacker-controlled domain git-tanstack.com used to host the transformers.pyz second-stage payload in the guardrails-ai 0.10.1 (CVE-2026-45758) and parallel TanStack/Mistral mini-Shai-Hulud campaign. Rationale: git-tanstack.com is the exact attacker domain identified by SafeDep, Qualys and Ox Security as the staging host for the TeamPCP campaign's transformers.pyz payload — the name typosquats the legitimate TanStack open-source org. Any successful resolution from inside the enterprise indicates either active compromise or sandbox detonation. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/mass-npm-supply-chain-attack-tanstack-mistral/ • https://qualysec.com/cybersecurity-news/mini-shai-hulud-worm-compromises/ • https://www.ox.security/blog/shai-hulud-here-we-go-again-170-packages-hit-across-npm-pypi/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","safari") and AccountName has_any ("ir-","secops-","threat-intel-","sandbox-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName making the lookup — a python* process is high-confidence compromise; a browser is likely analyst triage. 2) Contain: block the domain and 83.142.209.194 at egress/web proxy, isolate any non-analyst host that resolved it, and rotate developer credentials reachable from those hosts. 3) Hunt: pivot DNS log on `83.142.209.194` and adjacent /24 (`83.142.209.0/24`) for other TeamPCP infrastructure, cross-reference against any guardrails-ai install or transformers.pyz execution detections (UC1, UC2) on the same host within ±10 minutes.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] GlassFish java process spawning command shell (CVE-2026-2587 RCE) · [LLM] Inbound HTTP request to GlassFish gadget.jsf handler (CVE-2026-2587 exploit attempt) · [LLM] GlassFish java process outbound HTTP fetch to external host (gadget XML callback) · [LLM] Unpatched GlassFish admingui/jsftemplating inventory (CVE-2026-2587 attack surface)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
GlassFish java process spawning command shell (CVE-2026-2587 RCE) AIExploitation High
Detects the GlassFish admin console java process spawning a command interpreter or LOLBin child — the post-exploitation pivot after EL injection via gadget.jsf evaluates Runtime.exec(). Parent is matched on glassfish/asadmin/domain1 markers in its commandline so we don't fire on every JVM on the host. Rationale: Anchors on the GlassFish-specific parent (java + glassfish/asadmin/domain1/com.sun.aas.installRoot tokens documented in the Eclipse GlassFish startup args) plus an interpreter/LOLBin child — the exact RCE pivot the EL injection at /common/gadgets/gadget.jsf achieves via java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec(). Cross-checked Bhanunamikaze PoC repo and stack.watch advisory for exploit chain shape. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/Bhanunamikaze/CVE-2026-2587-Exploit-POC • https://stack.watch/vuln/CVE-2026-2587/ • https://app.opencve.io/cve/CVE-2026-2587 • https://blog.mindedsecurity.com/2015/11/reliable-os-shell-with-el-expression.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • GlassFish startup/shutdown scripts using cmd.exe /c or sh -c to invoke asadmin or perform pre/post lifecycle tasks
  • Deployed J2EE applications that legitimately use Runtime.exec / ProcessBuilder to call native binaries (e.g. ImageMagick wrappers, scheduled batch ingestion jobs)
  • Sysadmin running asadmin from a wrapper shell during maintenance (asadmin → sh → asadmin tree)
  • Java diagnostic tooling such as jcmd, jstack, or jstat invoked via shell from monitoring agents
  • GlassFish cluster sync scripts that wrap asadmin with bash on Linux deployments
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("list-applications","list-domains","start-domain","stop-domain","deploy --","undeploy --","asadmin.bat","asadmin.sh") and ParentCmd has "asadmin")
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("jcmd","jstack","jstat","jinfo") and ParentCmd has "glassfish")
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the full process tree for the java parent (PID, full ParentCommandLine, domain dir, listening ports). Confirm host runs Eclipse GlassFish < 7.1.0 / admingui < 8.0.2 / jsftemplating < 4.2.0. Inspect the child cmdline for reconnaissance (whoami, id, ifconfig) or staging (curl/wget pulling binaries). 2) Contain — isolate the host via Defender Live Response or EDR network containment, kill the suspect java domain process, snapshot the GlassFish domain1/logs directory and server.log, and block port 4848 ingress at the perimeter pending patch. 3) Hunt — pivot on the java PID for outbound HTTP fetches to non-corp IPs in the same window (UC3), search /common/gadgets/gadget.jsf access in upstream web/proxy logs (UC2), and check DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities for additional CVE-2026-2587-affected hosts (UC4).

| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("glassfish","asadmin","appserver-rt","domain1","com.sun.aas.installRoot")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","python.exe","sh","bash","dash","zsh")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,

          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where ParentProcessName has "java"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("glassfish","asadmin","appserver-rt","domain1","com.sun.aas.installRoot")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","python.exe")

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"

Inbound HTTP request to GlassFish gadget.jsf handler (CVE-2026-2587 exploit attempt) AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests targeting the vulnerable /common/gadgets/gadget.jsf endpoint with the gadget= URL parameter, the entry point for the EL injection RCE. Any external-sourced hit on this path is treatable as an exploit attempt because the admin console should not be internet-exposed. Rationale: The Bhanunamikaze PoC and Eclipse advisory both confirm the entry point is /common/gadgets/gadget.jsf with a gadget= URL parameter pointing to attacker-hosted XML — that string pair is a binary indicator that a CVE-2026-2587 attempt is in flight. EvalIndicator splits inline EL (URL contains #{ or %23%7B) from the callback-fetch variant where the EL lives in the fetched XML's ModulePrefs title attribute. Defender XDR is left empty because Defender Advanced Hunting does not ingest GlassFish/Apache/NGINX web access logs by default. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/Bhanunamikaze/CVE-2026-2587-Exploit-POC • https://stack.watch/vuln/CVE-2026-2587/ • https://www.hackingdream.net/2026/05/cve-2026-2587-glassfish-el-injection-exploit-poc.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal admin/operator legitimately using the gadget dashboard from a corporate IP (admin console SHOULD be internal-only — investigate the exposure even if benign)
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanners (Qualys, Nessus, Tenable Nessus Pro, Rapid7 InsightVM) probing CVE-2026-2587 from a known scanner ASN
  • Internal security team running the CVE-2026-2587 PoC validator from a sanctioned test host
  • Synthetic monitoring / uptime checks that crawl admin endpoints
  • Backup of the admin console performed via wget mirroring from a jump host
Suppression filter
// in CommonSecurityLog branch, suppress known scanners & internal admin jumps
| where not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Rapid7","Tenable","Acunetix","Nuclei","Burp"))
| where SourceIP !startswith "10." and SourceIP !startswith "192.168." and not (SourceIP matches regex @"^172\.(1[6-9]|2\d|3[0-1])\.")
Response runbook
1) Triage — extract gadget= parameter, URL-decode it. If it resolves to an external host or contains EL syntax (#{, %23%7B, java.lang.Runtime), treat as confirmed exploit attempt. Check upstream WAF for the source IP's request history and reputation (AbuseIPDB, threat intel). Pull the GlassFish host's java process tree for the same window. 2) Contain — block the source IP at the perimeter / WAF, remove /common/gadgets/gadget.jsf exposure (WAF rule or reverse-proxy deny), force-rotate any admin-console credentials, and disable the gadget handler if unused (upgrade or set the GlassFish admingui module to >= 8.0.2). 3) Hunt — correlate with UC1 process-tree alerts for the same host within ±10 min, look for the host's outbound fetches to the URL inside the gadget= param (UC3), search auth logs for successful admin-console logins from the same source IP preceding the exploit attempt.
(union isfuzzy=true
    (CommonSecurityLog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where RequestURL has "/common/gadgets/gadget.jsf"
     | where RequestURL has "gadget="
     | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, ResultDescription),
    (W3CIISLog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where csUriStem =~ "/common/gadgets/gadget.jsf"
     | where csUriQuery has "gadget="
     | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP = cIP, DestinationHostName = Computer, RequestURL = strcat(csUriStem, "?", csUriQuery), RequestMethod = csMethod, RequestClientApplication = csUserAgent, ResultDescription = tostring(scStatus)),
    (ImWebSession
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where Url has "/common/gadgets/gadget.jsf"
     | where Url has "gadget="
     | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP = SrcIpAddr, DestinationHostName = DstHostname, RequestURL = Url, RequestMethod = HttpMethod, RequestClientApplication = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, ResultDescription = tostring(HttpStatusCode)))
| extend GadgetParam = extract(@"(?i)gadget=([^&]+)", 1, RequestURL)
| extend EvalIndicator = iif(RequestURL has_any ("%23%7B","%23%7b","#{","getRuntime","java.lang.Runtime","ProcessBuilder","forName"), "DirectEL", "CallbackFetch")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: c9a5b7d8-1e43-6f78-a05c-3b6d4e0f1234

OR match(gadget_url,"^https?://(?!.*\.corp\.example\.com)") | sort 0 -lastTime
GlassFish java process outbound HTTP fetch to external host (gadget XML callback) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the GlassFish admin console java process fetching content from a public IP — the out-of-band step where the gadget handler retrieves the attacker-controlled XML payload to evaluate. Anchored on parent java + glassfish tokens to avoid the every-JVM-phones-home noise floor. Rationale: The CVE-2026-2587 exploit chain explicitly requires the GlassFish gadget handler to fetch the attacker-hosted XML from the URL in the gadget= parameter (per the Bhanunamikaze PoC, which hosts a benign probe XML and waits for the callback). A java process whose parent commandline carries the GlassFish startup tokens reaching out to a public IP on web ports is the network-side signature of that fetch. Tier set to hunting because legitimate Java integrations also call externally; pair with UC1 process-tree hits on the same host for high-confidence triage. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/Bhanunamikaze/CVE-2026-2587-Exploit-POC • https://stack.watch/vuln/CVE-2026-2587/
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • GlassFish phoning home for Java auto-update / telemetry to oracle.com / java.com
  • Deployed J2EE applications making legitimate REST calls to SaaS APIs (Salesforce, ServiceNow, payment gateways)
  • Maven Central / dependency-resolution fetches at GlassFish domain startup
  • License-server check-ins to vendor endpoints
  • Cluster sync between GlassFish nodes traversing a NAT'd public IP
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl endswith ".oracle.com" or RemoteUrl endswith ".java.com" or RemoteUrl endswith ".eclipse.org")
| where not (RemoteUrl endswith "maven.org" or RemoteUrl endswith ".sonatype.com" or RemoteUrl endswith "repo1.maven.org")
Response runbook
1) Triage — check whether the destination IP/host is a known corporate dependency (Java update, vendor SaaS, license server). Lookup reputation (VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB, urlscan). Pull the gadget.jsf access in upstream web logs for the same host within ±5 min (UC2) — a paired hit confirms the callback chain. 2) Contain — if destination is untrusted: isolate the GlassFish host, kill the java domain process, block the destination IP at egress, and capture the GlassFish server.log to identify the gadget= URL that triggered the fetch. 3) Hunt — pivot on the destination IP across all hosts to find other compromised GlassFish nodes, search DNS for the attacker domain across the fleet, and query DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities for CVE-2026-2587 affected hosts (UC4) to scope unpatched attack surface.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("glassfish","asadmin","appserver-rt","domain1","com.sun.aas.installRoot")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Hits = count(), Cmds = make_set(InitiatingProcessCommandLine, 5), URLs = make_set(RemoteUrl, 10)
          by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by LastSeen desc
// Pivot: outbound proxy / CASB log of Java User-Agent from a known GlassFish host. Maintain GlassFishHosts watchlist of host names/IPs.
let GlassFishHosts = dynamic(["glassfish-prod-01","glassfish-prod-02"]);  // populate from CMDB
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CommunicationDirection =~ "Outbound"
   or DeviceVendor in~ ("Zscaler","Palo Alto Networks","Cisco","Symantec","Forcepoint","Netskope")
| where SourceHostName in~ (GlassFishHosts) or SourceIP in ("<glassfish-ip-1>","<glassfish-ip-2>")
| where RequestClientApplication has_any ("Java/","Apache-HttpClient/","Jersey/")
| where DestinationPort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| where DestinationIP !startswith "10." and DestinationIP !startswith "192.168."
   and not (DestinationIP matches regex @"^172\.(1[6-9]|2\d|3[0-1])\.")
   and not (DestinationHostName endswith ".corp.example.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| !cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| !cidr("127.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| join(query={#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(\\\\java\.exe|\/java)$/i | regex("(?i)(glassfish|asadmin|domain1)", field=CommandLine) | groupBy([aid, TargetProcessId], function=count())}, field=[aid, ContextProcessId], include=[TargetProcessId])

Unpatched GlassFish admingui/jsftemplating inventory (CVE-2026-2587 attack surface) AIExploitation High
Surface-level hunting query that lists hosts with Eclipse GlassFish admingui < 8.0.2 or jsftemplating < 4.2.0 installed so the SOC can drive patching and prioritise UC1-UC3 alerts by exposure. Pure inventory pivot — not a behavioural detection. Rationale: Article explicitly names the affected Maven packages and version ceilings (admingui < 8.0.2, jsftemplating < 4.2.0). Defender's TVM tables natively expose CVE-to-host mapping, making this the cleanest one-shot inventory query. Ordered by IsInternetFacing because that flag is the single biggest exploit-likelihood multiplier for this CVE. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-29wv-cv7p-xjc2 • https://github.com/eclipse-ee4j/glassfish/releases • https://app.opencve.io/cve/CVE-2026-2587
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM lag — recently-patched hosts still appearing in the table until next inventory sync (24-48h)
  • Air-gapped lab/QA GlassFish instances flagged but not actually exposed
  • Embedded GlassFish in vendor appliances where the vendor — not the customer — owns patching
  • Host has the JAR present on disk but the server is not running / port 4848 is firewalled off
Response runbook
1) Triage — sort the result by IsInternetFacing == true and PublicIP isnotempty first; cross-reference with external attack-surface scans (Shodan, internal EASM) to confirm port 4848 / gadget.jsf reachability. 2) Contain — for any internet-exposed instance, immediately block 4848 ingress at the perimeter, disable the gadget handler at the reverse proxy (deny /common/gadgets/), and rotate admin-console credentials. For internal-only, schedule the upgrade to GlassFish 7.1.0+ / admingui 8.0.2+ / jsftemplating 4.2.0+ within the standard critical-patch SLA. 3) Hunt — for every host on this list, retro-hunt UC1/UC2/UC3 over the last 30 days to confirm no prior exploitation, and add the hostname/IP to the GlassFishHosts watchlist used in UC3 for ongoing high-confidence alerting.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-2587"
   or (SoftwareVendor =~ "eclipse" and SoftwareName has_any ("glassfish","admingui","jsftemplating"))
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| extend VulnerableComponent = case(
    SoftwareName has "admingui", "admingui < 8.0.2",
    SoftwareName has "jsftemplating", "jsftemplating < 4.2.0",
    SoftwareName has "glassfish", "glassfish < 7.1.0",
    "unknown")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, PublicIP, IsInternetFacing, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerableComponent, CveId, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc

   or (SoftwareVendor =~ "eclipse" and SoftwareName has_any ("glassfish","admingui","jsftemplating"))
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| extend VulnerableComponent = case(
    SoftwareName has "admingui", "admingui < 8.0.2",
    SoftwareName has "jsftemplating", "jsftemplating < 4.2.0",
    SoftwareName has "glassfish", "glassfish < 7.1.0",
    "unknown")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, OSPlatform, PublicIP, IsInternetFacing, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerableComponent, CveId, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc

   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Apache Camel JVM spawning shell or command interpreter via camel-exec (CVE-2026-47323 post-exploit) · [LLM] Apache Camel JVM writing files to sensitive paths via camel-file (CVE-2026-47323 arbitrary file write)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Inbound HTTP request with Camel-internal header or query param to CXF/Knative endpoint (CVE-2026-47323) AIExploitation High
Hunts for unauthenticated HTTP requests carrying Camel-reserved header names (CamelExecCommandExecutable, CamelFileName, CamelExecCommandArgs, etc.) destined for CXF-REST/CXF-SOAP/Knative-HTTP endpoints. Because the vulnerable HeaderFilterStrategy implementations only filter outbound — never inbound — any incoming HTTP request that smuggles a Camel-internal header through to a downstream camel-exec or camel-file route can override the configured executable or file path, yielding RCE or arbitrary file write. Rationale: The Camel-internal header names listed in the GHSA (CamelExecCommandExecutable, CamelFileName) are highly specific reserved strings — they only appear in legitimate traffic when a trusted Camel route forwards an internal message, which never crosses the wire from an external client in a correctly-segmented deployment. Any inbound HTTP request carrying these tokens to a CXF or Knative endpoint is a high-fidelity exploit attempt. Cross-checked against the Apache Camel security advisory page and the prior related CVEs cited in the GHSA (CVE-2025-30177, CVE-2025-27636, CVE-2025-29891, CVE-2026-40453) — all share the same header-injection primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://camel.apache.org/security/security-advisories.html • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-27636 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-29891 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8364-hfqj-pwm6
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal integration tests that POST Camel routes to themselves with internal headers as part of a regression suite.
  • Developer-facing diagnostic endpoints exposing Camel exchange dumps where reserved-header names appear in URL-encoded debug bodies.
  • Legitimate Camel-to-Camel federation traffic across a service mesh where the WAF is sniffing east-west traffic.
  • Security scanners (Nessus, Burp, Nuclei) running the CVE-2026-47323 check signature against your own assets — recognise scanner UAs and the CVE template ID.
Suppression filter
| where not(RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nessus", "Nuclei", "Burp", "Qualys", "Tenable")) and not(SourceIP in ("<internal-ci-runner-cidr>")) and DestinationHostName !startswith "camel-dev-"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: extract the SourceIP, RequestURL, full header set, and Camel header value. Confirm the destination is a Camel CXF-REST/CXF-SOAP/Knative-HTTP endpoint by checking the route definition for the URI path. Verify deployed Camel version against affected ranges (3.18.0–<4.14.6, 4.15.0–<4.18.2). Step 2 — Contain: if the deployed version is vulnerable, block the source IP at the perimeter and add a WAF rule denying any inbound request whose header or URL contains the `Camel*` reserved namespace (case-insensitive). For active exploitation, isolate the Camel JVM host. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the host to look for java.exe / java spawning cmd.exe / sh / powershell (camel-exec abuse) and for unusual file writes by the JVM to web roots, /tmp, or autorun paths (camel-file abuse) over the last 30 days. Pull thread/heap dumps before restart for forensics.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where RemotePort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443, 9000, 9080, 9443)
| where AdditionalFields has_any ("CamelExecCommandExecutable", "CamelFileName", "CamelExecCommandArgs", "CamelExecCommandWorkingDir", "CamelFileAbsolutePath", "CamelHttpQuery")
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("CamelExecCommandExecutable", "CamelFileName", "CamelExecCommandArgs")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe", "java", "javaw.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("camel", "cxf", "knative")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where RequestURL has_any ("CamelExecCommandExecutable", "CamelFileName", "CamelExecCommandArgs", "CamelExecCommandWorkingDir", "CamelFileAbsolutePath", "CamelHttpQuery")
   or Message has_any ("CamelExecCommandExecutable", "CamelFileName", "CamelExecCommandArgs", "CamelExecCommandWorkingDir", "CamelFileAbsolutePath", "CamelHttpQuery")
   or RequestCookies has_any ("CamelExecCommandExecutable", "CamelFileName")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourcePort, SourceHostName, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct, DeviceVendor, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Apache Camel CXF/Knative Inbound Header Injection (CVE-2026-47323)
id: 8c4d2f1a-7b3e-4f9a-9c5d-2e8b1a6f3d47
status: experimental
description: Detects HTTP requests containing Camel-internal header names (CamelExecCommandExecutable, CamelFileName, etc.) which CXF and Knative HeaderFilterStrategy implementations fail to filter inbound, enabling RCE or arbitrary file write via camel-exec / camel-file routes.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8364-hfqj-pwm6
  - https://camel.apache.org/security/CVE-2026-47323.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/04
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059
  - cve.2026.47323

      - 'CamelExecCommandArgs'

      - 'CamelFileAbsolutePath'
      - 'CamelHttpQuery'
  condition: selection_header
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate Camel-internal route testing where developers explicitly post Camel headers from one trusted endpoint to another.
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:linux.auditd OR source:nginx OR source:apache.httpd) (@http.url:(*CamelExecCommandExecutable* OR *CamelFileName* OR *CamelExecCommandArgs* OR *CamelExecCommandWorkingDir* OR *CamelFileAbsolutePath*) OR @http.useragent:(*CamelExecCommandExecutable* OR *CamelFileName*) OR @message:(*CamelExecCommandExecutable* OR *CamelFileName* OR *CamelExecCommandArgs*))

WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as url values(Web.http_method) as http_method values(Web.http_user_agent) as ua values(Web.src) as src values(Web.dest) as dest from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*CamelExecCommandExecutable*" OR Web.url="*CamelFileName*" OR Web.url="*CamelExecCommandArgs*" OR Web.url="*CamelExecCommandWorkingDir*" OR Web.url="*CamelFileAbsolutePath*" OR Web.url="*CamelHttpQuery*" OR Web.http_user_agent="*CamelExecCommandExecutable*" OR Web.http_referrer="*CamelExecCommandExecutable*") by Web.dest Web.src Web.url Web.http_method Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as url values(Web.http_method) as http_method values(Web.http_user_agent) as ua values(Web.src) as src values(Web.dest) as dest from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*CamelExecCommandExecutable*" OR Web.url="*CamelFileName*" OR Web.url="*CamelExecCommandArgs*" OR Web.url="*CamelExecCommandWorkingDir*" OR Web.url="*CamelFileAbsolutePath*" OR Web.url="*CamelHttpQuery*" OR Web.http_user_agent="*CamelExecCommandExecutable*" OR Web.http_referrer="*CamelExecCommandExecutable*") by Web.dest Web.src Web.url Web.http_method Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Apache Camel JVM spawning shell or command interpreter via camel-exec (CVE-2026-47323 post-exploit) AIInstallation High
Detects java/javaw processes hosting Camel routes spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, sh, bash, or LOLBin children — the post-exploitation footprint of CamelExecCommandExecutable header injection. The camel-exec component reads its target binary from the Camel exchange header at runtime; when the attacker controls that header, the JVM literally execs whatever they specify, so this parent→child shape is the cleanest behavioural signal after the wire-side filter is bypassed. Rationale: Java spawning cmd.exe/sh/LOLBin children is already an unusual pattern in production; combined with a parent command line containing 'camel', 'cxf', 'knative', or '-jar' running a Camel artifact, the FP rate collapses. This is the deterministic execution shape of camel-exec when CamelExecCommandExecutable is attacker-controlled per the GHSA. Cross-checked Camel docs for camel-exec processor behaviour and the prior CVE-2025-30177 (camel-undertow) advisory which describes the same RCE end-state. Cross-checked against: • https://camel.apache.org/components/latest/exec-component.html • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-30177 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8364-hfqj-pwm6
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Build agents (Jenkins/GitLab runners) where Maven or Gradle invocations shell out to git, openssl, or curl as part of a build step.
  • Camel routes that intentionally use camel-exec with a static, hard-coded executable for batch processing (e.g. invoking ffmpeg or a custom binary).
  • Application Performance Monitoring (APM) agents (Dynatrace, AppDynamics) that periodically launch shell helpers from within the JVM.
  • Java-based installers (IzPack, install4j) launching cmd.exe as part of first-run configuration on application servers.
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jenkins", "gitlab-runner", "maven", "gradle", "dynatrace", "appdynamics")) and not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\Jenkins\\", "\\gitlab-runner\\", "\\.m2\\", "\\.gradle\\"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: capture the child process command line and SHA256, and the parent java command line (jar path identifies the Camel application). Pivot to the network log around the same timestamp to find the inbound HTTP request that carried the malicious Camel header. Step 2 — Contain: kill the JVM child chain and isolate the host. Disable the affected Camel route at the management console; if not possible, stop the JVM service. Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate all java→shell parent/child pairs across the estate over the last 30 days, filter to JVMs running a Camel application, and treat any historical hits as candidate compromises. Pull JVM heap dumps before restart to recover the in-memory Camel exchange that triggered the exec.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe", "javaw.exe", "java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("camel", "cxf", "knative", "-jar")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "sh", "bash", "dash", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "rundll32.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe", "curl.exe", "wget", "mshta.exe", "regsvr32.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\java.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\javaw.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "/java"
| where NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/sh" or NewProcessName endswith "/bash" or NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\certutil.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\bitsadmin.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\rundll32.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Apache Camel JVM writing files to sensitive paths via camel-file (CVE-2026-47323 arbitrary file write) AIInstallation Medium
Detects java/javaw processes (Camel runtime) writing files into web roots, system directories, autorun locations, or SSH key paths — the file-write half of CVE-2026-47323 where attacker-controlled CamelFileName / CamelFileAbsolutePath headers override the configured camel-file producer destination. Pivots on the JVM as the writer with an article-specific path allow-list of high-value drop targets. Rationale: camel-file's producer resolves its destination from the CamelFileName / CamelFileAbsolutePath exchange header per Camel docs. The GHSA explicitly calls out camel-file as the second exploitation primitive after camel-exec. The JVM writing JSP/WAR/ASPX or authorized_keys into a webroot or autorun path is a high-fidelity arbitrary-file-write signal regardless of the underlying CVE — pairing the path/extension allow-list with the JVM-as-writer pivot makes this article-specific. Verified against Apache Camel file-component documentation and CVE-2025-29891 advisory (same primitive in camel-undertow). Cross-checked against: • https://camel.apache.org/components/latest/file-component.html • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-29891 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8364-hfqj-pwm6
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1547.001 T1098.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Camel applications legitimately writing log files or processed messages to a configured directory that overlaps with the path allow-list (e.g. an app server writing to its own /webapps).
  • Tomcat/Jetty hot-deployment of WAR files dropped by a Java-based CI deployer co-located on the host.
  • Java-based backup agents writing scheduled task XMLs or cron entries as part of legitimate maintenance.
  • Java-based config-management agents (e.g. Puppet Java client) writing scripts to /etc/cron.* during scheduled runs.
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has_any ("\\camel-app-logs\\", "\\processed\\", "\\outbox\\")) and not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("puppet", "chef", "ansible"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: review TargetFilePath and the file content (pull the file hash and inspect contents) — a freshly-dropped JSP/WAR/ASPX in a web root with non-standard content is almost certainly a web shell. Correlate timestamp with inbound WAF/CommonSecurityLog for a request carrying CamelFileName. Step 2 — Contain: quarantine the dropped file, isolate the host, and disable the Camel route. If the file is a web shell, capture forensic copies before deletion. Step 3 — Hunt: search every JVM in the estate for file writes to the same path allow-list over 90 days; for each hit, validate whether the writing route had inbound HTTP exposure. Audit all camel-file producer routes for trusted-header assumptions and patch to 4.14.6/4.18.2/4.19.0.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe", "javaw.exe", "java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("camel", "cxf", "knative", "-jar")
| where (FolderPath has_any ("\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\", "\\webapps\\", "\\htdocs\\", "/var/www/", "/usr/share/nginx/", "\\Startup\\", "\\System32\\", "\\SysWOW64\\", "/etc/cron", "/.ssh/", "\\Windows\\Tasks\\", "\\AppData\\Roaming\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\"))
   or (FileName endswith ".jsp" or FileName endswith ".jspx" or FileName endswith ".war" or FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".sh" or FileName endswith ".bat" or FileName endswith ".ps1" or FileName =~ "authorized_keys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where ActingProcessName endswith "\\java.exe" or ActingProcessName endswith "\\javaw.exe" or ActingProcessName endswith "/java"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("camel", "cxf", "knative", "-jar")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\", "\\webapps\\", "/var/www/", "/usr/share/nginx/", "\\Startup\\", "\\System32\\", "/etc/cron", "/.ssh/", "\\Windows\\Tasks\\")
   or TargetFileExtension in~ ("jsp", "jspx", "war", "aspx", "php", "sh", "bat", "ps1")

[GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-45568: rok Python ProxyShare can be used as an SSRF proxy through absolute URL paths

GitHub Security Advisories
2026-05-19 2 use cases 0 techniques 2 kill-chain phases detected

rok Python ProxyShare can be used as an SSRF proxy through absolute URL paths

CVEsCVE-2026-45568

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] zrok ProxyShare SSRF — request path begins with absolute URL (CVE-2026-45568)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
zrok ProxyShare SSRF — request path begins with absolute URL (CVE-2026-45568) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to a zrok Python ProxyShare where the request path itself is an absolute URL (http:// or https://) — the precise shape of the CVE-2026-45568 SSRF, including pivots to cloud metadata services like 127.0.0.1:19190/metadata. Article-specific because Flask + urllib.parse.urljoin only rewrites the host when the second argument is absolute, so this URI shape is the exact attacker vector. Rationale: Article specifies the exact SSRF primitive: a request path that itself is an absolute URL (e.g. http://127.0.0.1:19190/metadata) bypasses urljoin's base-URL anchoring. The Sentinel union targets the two web-server log tables actually populated for App Service and IIS-hosted zrok deployments; the Defender query pivots on the resulting outbound proxy call to link-local / loopback metadata IPs since Defender doesn't expose web access logs. Cross-checked GHSA-jh67-hwqw-m5r7 and the urllib.parse.urljoin RFC-3986 absolute-URI behaviour documented at docs.python.org. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jh67-hwqw-m5r7 • https://docs.python.org/3/library/urllib.parse.html#urllib.parse.urljoin • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-45568
ATT&CKT1190 T1090
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate forward-proxy clients sending RFC 7230 §5.3.2 absolute-URI request lines (rare on reverse-proxy shares but possible from old proxies and curl --proxy)
  • Synthetic monitoring / DAST tooling (Burp, ZAP, Qualys) probing the share for SSRF as part of authorised testing
  • Health-check probes that intentionally request the loopback metadata endpoint to verify the share is reachable
  • Misconfigured CDN / WAF that URL-encodes then double-decodes the path producing a stem that looks like an absolute URL
  • Internal red-team validating the patch for CVE-2026-45568
Suppression filter
// Suppress known-good scanners and health probes
| where UserAgent !has_any ("HealthCheck","Pingdom","StatusCake","AlwaysOn","AzureFunctionsRuntime")
| where ClientIP !in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
// Exclude double-decoded false stems where the absolute URL is actually under a known safe prefix
| where not (UriStem startswith "/proxy/" and UserAgent has "corp-dast-scanner")
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Pivot on `ClientIP` and the full UriStem/UriQuery — confirm the path really begins with http:// or https:// or targets a cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254, 100.100.100.200, metadata.google.internal). Capture the `_ResourceId` to identify which zrok share is exposed. 2. CONTAIN: Stop the affected zrok share (`zrok release <share-token>`) or block the source IP at the front-door WAF. Rotate any cloud instance credentials reachable via metadata from the host running zrok, since IMDS exfil may already have occurred. Upgrade zrok to >1.1.11 per the GHSA. 3. HUNT: Query DeviceNetworkEvents (or NetworkConnectIP4) for the share-host's outbound connections to 169.254.169.254 / 127.0.0.1 in the same window; pull any `requests` / urllib traffic from python processes; review CloudTrail / Azure Activity for new role-assumptions or temporary-credential issuance from the host's instance-profile role.
// Defender Advanced Hunting has no native web-server log table; this detection lives in IIS / AppService / WAF logs and is expressed on Sentinel side.
// Closest Defender pivot: any process on a zrok-hosting endpoint making an outbound connection to a link-local / loopback metadata IP shortly after receiving inbound traffic on the share.
let MetadataIPs = dynamic(["127.0.0.1","169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2","fd00:ec2::254","100.100.100.200"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("zrok.exe","zrok","python.exe","python3","python","pythonw.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("zrok share","ProxyShare","zrok.proxy","urllib.parse.urljoin")
| where RemoteIP in (MetadataIPs) or RemoteIP startswith "169.254."
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
// Hunt inbound HTTP requests where the URI itself is an absolute URL (the zrok ProxyShare SSRF shape).
let Lookback = 7d;
let AbsoluteUrlPath = @"(?i)^/+https?:/";
let MetadataMarkers = dynamic(["127.0.0.1","169.254.169.254","metadata.google","metadata.azure","100.100.100.200","/metadata","/latest/meta-data","/computeMetadata"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(
    W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
    | where csUriStem matches regex AbsoluteUrlPath
         or csUriQuery has_any (MetadataMarkers)
    | project TimeGenerated, _ResourceId, Computer,
              ClientIP = cIP, Method = csMethod,
              UriStem = csUriStem, UriQuery = csUriQuery,
              Status = scStatus, UserAgent = csUserAgent,
              SourceTable = "W3CIISLog"
),
(
    AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
    | where CsUriStem matches regex AbsoluteUrlPath
         or CsUriQuery has_any (MetadataMarkers)
    | project TimeGenerated, _ResourceId, Computer = CsHost,
              ClientIP = CIp, Method = CsMethod,
              UriStem = CsUriStem, UriQuery = CsUriQuery,
              Status = ScStatus, UserAgent = UserAgent,
              SourceTable = "AppServiceHTTPLogs"
)
| extend AbsoluteUrlInPath = iff(UriStem matches regex AbsoluteUrlPath, true, false)
| extend MetadataTargeted = iff(UriStem has_any (MetadataMarkers) or UriQuery has_any (MetadataMarkers), true, false)
| where AbsoluteUrlInPath or MetadataTargeted
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] HAXcms CVE-2026-46395: vulnerable @haxtheweb/haxcms-nodejs <= 25.0.0 present
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] HAXcms CVE-2026-46395: unauthenticated GET to /system/api/connectionSettings · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-46395: HAXcms: Private Key Disclosure via Broken HMAC

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] HAXcms CVE-2026-46395: forged-JWT admin write within 30m of connectionSettings leak
HAXcms CVE-2026-46395: unauthenticated GET to /system/api/connectionSettings AIExploitation High
Surfaces any HTTP GET to the HAXcms unauthenticated /system/api/connectionSettings endpoint, which returns base64 tokens whose tail bytes are the private signing key (privateKey+salt) plaintext. A single GET against a vulnerable @haxtheweb/haxcms-nodejs <= 25.0.0 instance fully discloses the JWT-signing secret, so any request to this path on internet-facing HAXcms deployments warrants triage. Rationale: Endpoint path `/system/api/connectionSettings` is the article-named primary leak vector and is not present on benign HAXcms traffic that goes through the authenticated UI. A successful 2xx on this path is essentially equivalent to private-key exfiltration. Defender_kql is intentionally empty because Defender Advanced Hunting does not ship raw HTTP request URIs for arbitrary Node.js applications — the detection lives on the web tier (AppServiceHTTPLogs / W3CIISLog). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6c8g-9hfh-pq5h • https://github.com/haxtheweb/issues
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised internal/external penetration test enumerating the HAXcms endpoints
  • Vulnerability scanners (Tenable / Qualys / Nuclei) probing this exact CVE template after public disclosure
  • HAXcms development / staging instances being smoke-tested by the maintainer
  • Legitimate HAXcms CLI tooling that hits connectionSettings as part of provisioning (only seen from internal IPs)
Suppression filter
| where SourceIp !in ("<internal_scanner_ip>", "<pentest_jumpbox_ip>")
| where UserAgent !has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Nuclei", "Burp", "sqlmap")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the host is running @haxtheweb/haxcms-nodejs <= 25.0.0 (vulnerable). Pull the response size from the web log — a 2xx with >100 byte body indicates the key was returned. Geo/ASN the source IP and check whether the user-agent matches a known scanner. Step 2 (contain): If response was 2xx, treat the private signing key as compromised. Isolate the HAXcms host from the internet, rotate the signing key + salt, invalidate all outstanding admin/user/site tokens, force re-authentication, and patch to a fixed version once available. Step 3 (hunt): Look back 30 days on the same host for any prior GETs to /system/api/connectionSettings from external IPs, and for any subsequent authenticated admin writes (saveOutline / saveManifest / saveNode / createSite / deleteSite / file uploads) from the same source IP — the forged-JWT chain produces no login events.
let WindowDays = 7d;
let HaxcmsLeak = union isfuzzy=true
    (AppServiceHTTPLogs
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(WindowDays)
        | where csMethod =~ "GET"
        | where csUriStem =~ "/system/api/connectionSettings"
        | project TimeGenerated, SourceIp = CIp, Host = CsHost, UriStem = csUriStem, Method = csMethod, Status = ScStatus, UserAgent),
    (W3CIISLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(WindowDays)
        | where csMethod =~ "GET"
        | where csUriStem =~ "/system/api/connectionSettings"
        | project TimeGenerated, SourceIp = cIP, Host = sSiteName, UriStem = csUriStem, Method = csMethod, Status = scStatus, UserAgent = csUserAgent);
HaxcmsLeak
| where Status between (200 .. 299)   // 2xx = key successfully disclosed
| summarize Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 10), Statuses = make_set(Status, 5)
            by SourceIp, Host
| order by FirstSeen desc

HAXcms CVE-2026-46395: forged-JWT admin write within 30m of connectionSettings leak AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates a successful GET to /system/api/connectionSettings (the private-key leak primitive) with subsequent authenticated HAXcms admin-write API calls from the same source IP within 30 minutes. Because forged JWTs are signed with the stolen privateKey+salt they produce no login events and look indistinguishable from the real admin to single-event detections — this temporal correlation is the cleanest way to catch the full exploit chain. Rationale: The article describes the complete exploit chain (extract key → forge admin JWT → call admin API) as feasible "with a single HTTP request" sequence, and explicitly warns the forged tokens "produce no login events in logs". Temporal correlation of the article-named leak path (`/system/api/connectionSettings`) with the article-named admin endpoints (saveOutline / saveManifest / saveNode / createSite / deleteSite / saveFile / saveUser / form_token) from the same source IP within a tight window is the only reliable host-agnostic signal. Defender_kql is a host-tier approximation that depends on the HAXcms server itself being enrolled in Defender for Endpoint; if it is not, leave the Defender field empty operationally and rely on the Sentinel / Splunk web-tier queries. Datadog/Falcon/Sigma left empty — single-shape Sigma cannot express the cross-event join, and Falcon FDR does not ship arbitrary Node.js HTTP request URIs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6c8g-9hfh-pq5h • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-46395
ATT&CKT1606.001 T1078 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised pentester chaining the disclosure + write actions in a single engagement IP
  • Legitimate HAXcms admin behind a shared NAT egress that also happens to be a CI scanner that probes connectionSettings
  • Internal vulnerability validation by an AppSec engineer hitting both endpoints from the same workstation
  • Site backup/restore tooling that legitimately calls saveOutline/saveManifest after configuration reads
Suppression filter
| where SourceIp !in ("<internal_admin_workstation_ip>", "<pentest_egress_ip>")
| where UserAgent !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","Burp")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the leaking endpoint returned a 2xx response with non-trivial body size (>100 bytes). Examine the admin-write requests' Authorization header (if logged) — if the JWT's `iat` is suspiciously close to the leak time and `user` claim is `admin`, treat as confirmed forgery. Cross-check whether the genuine admin had an interactive session on Entra/Okta during the same window — absence is incriminating. Step 2 (contain): Take the HAXcms instance offline or block at the WAF, rotate `privateKey + salt`, invalidate every outstanding user_token / site_token / form_token / base_token by regenerating, force admin password reset, and snapshot site content for offline integrity comparison. Patch @haxtheweb/haxcms-nodejs above the fixed version. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the source IP across the WAF for the prior 30 days — same IP touching /system/api/connectionSettings on any other HAXcms tenant indicates active mass-exploitation.
